text:
Tens of thousands of homeowners face a payment shock as their adjustable-rate mortgages reset, per the WSJ.

About 186,000 ARMs are set to reset next year, according to data from ICE. The typical borrower’s payment will rise about $645 a month at the first reset.

The hardest hit are people who took out seven-year ARMs in 2020, when rates were near record lows. Their median monthly payment is set to jump 43%, or $1,269, with some going from rates below 3% to closer to 8%.

ARMs make up only about 5% of active mortgages, and today’s versions have more safeguards than those that fueled the 2008 crash.

Paul Tudor Jones: Almost Every Big Crash Has the Same Root Cause, Too Much Leverage Somewhere

If I think of some really, really big accidents, most of them have the same underlying reason, same underlying foundation, which is some too much leverage somewhere. Most of the leverage, most of the time, if I think of the big ones, were derivative inspired, either futures or options.

1987, that crash was 100% portfolio insurance, 100%. Had they had limits, which they didn't, it would have been a 10%, maybe 15% max, but that was 100% derivatives.

If I think about 1998, Long-Term Capital, big derivatives, they had a huge balance sheet with a lot of derivatives they were offsides on.

2000 was a little different. 2000 was the easiest bear market I've ever seen in my whole life. It's got so many similarities to right now in the sense that the bear market of 2001 and 2002 were a consequence of all the IPOs in 99, 2000, and then as they unlocked, you just had this never-ending cascade of selling.

🚨🇺🇸 Jensen Huang envisage de revenir à la tête de Nvidia.

Quelques jours seulement après sa démission

D'après le FT, il en a discuté avec ses proches. Et ses alliés montent une « war room » de patrons de la Silicon Valley pour faire pression sur le board

Objectif : obtenir aussi le soutien de la Maison Blanche.

La campagne a pris de l'ampleur ce week-end :
→ Elon Musk et Tim Sweeney (Epic Games) soutiennent la lettre ouverte « Bring Jensen Back »
→ Des employés de Nvidia la signent publiquement
→ Brad Gerstner (Altimeter) et Gavin Baker (Atreides), deux gros actionnaires, demandent au board de garder « toutes les options sur la table », y compris son retour

« Tout ce qui compte dans la tech, hors labs d'IA, adore Jensen », résume un de ses soutiens, dans ta gueule Dario 

Mais ça coince et ça risque en être très très dur 
→ Scott Bessent, secrétaire au Trésor, réclame un « grand ménage » à la tête de Nvidia
→ Le board mène une enquête indépendante
→ Jensen n'a pas le contrôle du capital, donc il ne peut pas passer outre le board. Il n’a que 3.4 ish %
→ Rene Haas, le patron d'Arm, aurait été approché comme successeur (le board dit qu'aucun processus « formel » n'est lancé)

Le vrai sujet pour le marché, c'est la conformité des ventes de puces en Asie, qui va être scrutée de très près, certains annoncent qu’ils ont gonflés les chiffres en Asie. 

Et tout ça arrive à deux jours des résultats, mardi, avec Colette Kress en intérim et l’IPO d’Anthropic Jeudi sous un fond macro

Now, maybe the good news is more of those carriers will offer ACA plans in more states because there's more money there. OK, you can make that argument.

But the reality is all it is is a revenue plan for the big carriers, which is not what I think they're trying to accomplish."

text:
The take that many NVIDIA supply deals were "a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract" is half right.

Jensen did made the big calls in the room. CEOs of some of NVIDIA's largest customers told me that this past week. Billion-dollar commitments, made on the spot. I'd bet suppliers saw the same. That is hard to replace.

What's overstated is the risk to the biggest deals. They're on paper.

• NVIDIA disclosed $279B in supply and capacity commitments as of July, up from $119B a quarter earlier, driven by memory. $267B of it is scheduled through fiscal 2029. You can’t report it without more than a handshake. 
• NVIDIA became TSMC's largest customer in 2025. The two biggest HBM suppliers are tightening contracts so buyers can't back out. Suppliers aren't the flight risk.
• I've said supply and the roadmap are mostly set for at least 18 months.

The real exposure is the next round: anything not on paper, and whether NVIDIA keeps committing at Jensen's pace. Rivals will bid for whatever it doesn't.

NVIDIA has a deep bench, and Colette Kress has been on calls reassuring suppliers. Tuesday's $NVDA call, her first as interim CEO, is where she shows who makes the big calls now.
